SPARCS enables scalable recovery of complex image-based phenotypes for genetic screening
abstract: Forward genetic screening links genotype to phenotype by introducing random genetic perturbations and identifying phenotype-altering mutations. Although genome-scale screens are routine for simple phenotypes in cultured cells, extending them to complex image-based phenotypes remains challenging. Here, we present spatially resolved CRISPR screening (SPARCS), a microscopy-based platform for forward genetic screening on single-cell images. SPARCS physically isolates mutants in situ by automated laser microdissection, enabling image-based screening at unprecedented scale with multimodal hit phenotyping. We demonstrate SPARCS in genome-wide CRISPR knockout screens of autophagosome formation and activation of the immune sensor STING across 70 million cells. Via machine learning-based image analysis, SPARCS recovered most macroautophagy genes and identified GPHR as a pH-dependent regulator of STING. Mass spectrometry-based proteomics of isolated hit cells revealed endoplasmic reticulum (ER)/Golgi disruption and nominated additional STING regulators via in silico perturbation modeling. These results establish SPARCS as a scalable platform for genome-wide genetic screening of complex cellular phenotypes with a proteome-level readout.

title: A non-canonical function of glutathione to suppress ferroptosis via FSP1
abstract: It is well established that glutathione (GSH) is mainly utilized by glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) to diminish peroxidized phospholipids and defend against ferroptosis. However, we found that GSH robustly protects a variety of GPX4 knockout (KO) cells from ferroptosis, thus indicating that there is an alternative pathway for GSH to suppress ferroptosis. By carrying out genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screening, we identified that ferroptosis suppressor protein 1 (FSP1) is the key factor mediating the GPX4-independent protective effect of GSH. Mechanistically, FSP1 uses GSH to generate reduced ubiquinone, which scavenges oxidized lipids and suppresses ferroptosis. Inhibition of FSP1 abolishes this GSH-dependent ferroptosis protection both in vitro and in vivo. Distinct from NAD(P)H-mediated ubiquinone reduction, GSH-stimulated generation of reduced ubiquinone via FSP1 is independent of flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD). Together, our work clarifies a new mechanism of GSH-mediated ferroptosis suppression, thus highlighting the potential that targeting GSH metabolism should be beneficial for ferroptosis-related diseases whether or not it is related to GPX4.

title: A spatiotemporal lifecycle atlas decodes spatial coordination in rice
abstract: How gene expression programs are coordinated across space and time to build a complete plant remains poorly understood. Here, we combine high-resolution spatial transcriptomics, single-nucleus RNA sequencing, and a gap-free reference genome to build a 3D spatiotemporal atlas of rice, spanning 10 organs and 61 stages from seed to seed. Our datasets profile 851,725 nuclei and 347,640 spatial bins, defining 119 cell types and 133 subtypes across the rice lifecycle. Through multimodal integration, we reconstruct an inferred developmental trajectory graph that links cell states from the proembryo to mature organs and identifies trajectory-associated regulators. We further implicate the pleiotropic regulator OsARF1 in distinct spatial gene programs across developmental contexts. We also uncover widespread axis-associated transcriptional asymmetry, including dorsoventral endosperm programs that partition starch and protein accumulation. Collectively, this high-resolution atlas provides a spatiotemporal framework for understanding rice development and guiding future crop improvement.

title: Cancer competition for vitamin B2 creates metabolic checkpoint for T cell ferroptosis
abstract: Metabolic competition between tumors and T cells drives immune evasion, but the transporters and mechanisms remain largely elusive. Here, we establish the CareSLCs platform and identify that SLC52A3-mediated vitamin B2 (VB2) uptake is indispensable for T cell antitumor immunity. Mechanistically, VB2 deficiency impairs mitochondrial respiration and glutathione regeneration, leading to mitophagy, labile iron accumulation, and lipid peroxidation that trigger T cell ferroptosis. Unexpectedly, tumors preferentially employ SLC52A2, not SLC52A3, to scavenge VB2 and outcompete T cells. Tumor SLC52A2 ablation enhances T cell function in immunocompetent hosts without appreciably affecting intrinsic tumor growth. Clinically, high tumoral SLC52A2 correlates with T cell dysfunction and poor survival, whereas dietary VB2 intake is associated with reduced cancer risks. Thus, VB2 supplementation or SLC52A3 overexpression augments CAR-T cell antitumor efficacy. Our results suggest that tumoral VB2 competition establishes a metabolic checkpoint driving T cell ferroptosis and that enhancing VB2 uptake reinvigorates T cells to improve cancer immunotherapy.

title: STING reprogramming by estrogen promotes neutrophil extracellular trap formation and sex-biased resistance to ADC therapy
abstract: Sex differences in cancer therapy response remain poorly understood. Using a "phase II-like preclinical trial" across 55 CLDN18.2 + pancreatic cancer patient-derived xenografts, we identify marked female-biased resistance to CLDN18.2-targeted antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) therapy despite equivalent antigen expression. Mechanistically, estrogen signals through GPER1 to upregulate TRAF6, redirecting tumor-intrinsic STING signaling from IRF3-mediated interferon production toward nuclear factor κB (NF-κB) activation. This drives CXCL1 secretion, neutrophil recruitment, and neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation. NETs form a charged extracellular network that restricts antibody access to tumor-cell-surface antigens-a mechanism we term functional antigen shielding-reducing ADC cytotoxicity independently of antigen expression. The NET burden also correlated with poorer responses to trastuzumab, cetuximab, and enfortumab vedotin across three clinical cohorts. Pharmacologic NET disruption with sivelestat restored ADC efficacy in female mice. These findings reveal an estrogen-driven resistance mechanism with broad implications for antibody-based cancer therapy.

title: A fluctuation test for gastruloid heterogeneity
abstract: Stem cells self-organize into models of early development, but even under carefully controlled conditions, the resulting organoids exhibit substantial "inter-individual" heterogeneity. To explore its origins, we generated monoclonal gastruloids, each derived from a single mouse embryonic stem cell (mESC). Molecular profiling revealed extensive heterogeneity: some gastruloids failed to develop, others were biased toward mesodermal or neural fates, and yet others contained cell types atypical of conventional polyclonal gastruloids. Applying DNA Typewriter, a cell lineage recorder, we identified heritable fate biases arising prior to gastruloid induction and found that more closely related founder mESCs give rise to more phenotypically similar gastruloids. Linking mESC subclones to their descendants' fates revealed cryptic, fate-predictive differences in gene expression and chromatin accessibility, including at imprinted, methylation-sensitive loci linked to developmental potency. Intrinsic, heritable fluctuations in mESC state are therefore an important source of organoid heterogeneity, and DNA Typewriter enables high-resolution lineage trees in stem cell models.

title: Arabidopsis uses distinct coumarins and bacterial pathways for pH-adaptive iron acquisition
abstract: Iron (Fe) limitation restricts plant growth in diverse soils, and root-associated microbes can alleviate plant Fe starvation. Whether plants integrate the edaphic environment and microbial activities into their Fe uptake strategies remains unclear. We show that bacterium-mediated alleviation of Fe deficiency in Arabidopsis functions at varying environmental pH and is taxonomically widespread among root microbiota isolates from soils with different edaphic profiles. This process is regulated by host-controlled and pH-adapted root exudation of different coumarin chemotypes. These exometabolites interact with root-associated bacteria to mobilize Fe either via bacterial siderophore-mediated chelation at circumneutral pH or redox-sensing-controlled, reduction-based pathways at acidic pH. The corresponding bacterial genes are prevalent in the root microbiota, and they likely evolved before the emergence of land plants. Our findings suggest that Fe malnutrition-induced exudation of redox-active metabolites by non-graminaceous plant species is a widespread adaptation for Fe mobilization from soil, mediated by the co-option of ancient microbial processes.

title: Immunoregulatory gene GIMAP6 suppresses lethal atherosclerotic vasculopathy and ischemic heart failure
abstract: Controlling hyperlipidemia has reduced but not eliminated atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) as a major cause of human mortality. Here, we report that loss of the immunoregulatory gene GTPase of immunity-associated protein 6 (Gimap6) in mice causes an inflammatory vasculopathy and accelerated atherosclerosis in the absence of hyperlipidemia. These vascular abnormalities cause progressive cardiac ischemia, myocardial infarction, and heart failure, culminating in early death. GIMAP6 loss precipitates early endothelial barrier failure and a mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS)-PPARγ-CD36 lipid-influx cascade that lowers the threshold for foam-cell formation and induces IL-6/MCP-1/TNF-mediated inflammation. Human hypomorphic GIMAP6 variants, including the African-ancestry-enriched V65I allele, are associated with altered monocyte redox balance, increased CD36-mediated lipid uptake, and early ASCVD. Thus, GIMAP6 is a crucial safeguard for vascular integrity that restrains endothelial dysfunction, macrophage foam cell generation, and inflammation that can cause lethal ASCVD independently of systemic hyperlipidemia.

title: Comprehensive lineage tracing maps the landscape of cell fate decisions in mouse embryogenesis
abstract: . Here, we use PEtracer to continuously install heritable genetic marks as cells divide, reconstructing lineage trees that resolve ~75% of cell divisions across >1.5 million cells from 16 mouse embryos collected at half-day intervals from E7.5-E10.0. We pair these trees with deep transcriptional profiling to chart the landscape of cell fate decisions during gastrulation and early organogenesis. Using these data, we quantify cell fate biases, restriction timing, progenitor pool sizes, and lineage relationships across the embryo, revealing strikingly reproducible lineage architecture across replicate embryos despite the regulative flexibility of mammalian development. We further show how lineage, spatial position, and signaling jointly determine fate outcomes and timing, with their relative influence varying by tissue. This dataset provides a quantitative framework for understanding cell fate specification and a lineage-resolved reference for generating and contextualizing developmental hypotheses at organismal scale.

title: Mapping transcriptional responses to cellular perturbations with RNA fingerprinting
abstract: Single-cell perturbation dictionaries measure how cells respond to genetic and chemical perturbations, creating the opportunity to assign causal interpretations to observational data. We introduce RNA fingerprinting, a statistical framework that maps transcriptional responses from new experiments onto reference perturbation dictionaries. RNA fingerprinting learns perturbation representations, or "fingerprints," from single-cell data, then probabilistically assigns query cells to one or more candidate perturbations. We benchmark on ground-truth datasets, demonstrating accurate assignments at single-cell resolution, scalability to genome-wide screens, and the ability to resolve combinatorial perturbations. We demonstrate broad utility across diverse biological settings: identifying context-specific regulators of p53 under ribosomal stress, characterizing dose-dependent drug mechanisms of action, and uncovering cytokine-driven B cell heterogeneity during secondary influenza infection in vivo. Together, these results establish RNA fingerprinting as a versatile framework for interpreting single-cell datasets by linking cellular states to their underlying perturbations.

title: Rare k-mers reveal centromere haplogroups underlying human diversity and cancer translocations
abstract: Abstract Centromeres are among the most diverse and dynamically evolving regions of the human genome and are commonly affected in various human cancers. However, organized into highly repetitive α-satellite higher-order repeats (HORs), human centromere sequences have long resisted detailed genomic analysis. Although the development of long-read sequencing platforms has enabled the analysis of complete centromere sequences, their application to a large set of samples is still largely limited, preventing our understanding of centromere variation and haplotype structures across large human populations and the structural basis of centromere-involving translocations in cancer. Here we show that rare k-mers present in centromeric regions can serve as effective markers for dissecting the complexity of centromere structure, particularly that of active α-satellite HOR arrays (aHOR arrays), across human populations and for understanding centromere-involving abnormalities in cancer. Based on rare k-mer-based clustering, centromere aHOR arrays are clustered into discrete haplogroups (aHOR-HGs) with distinct structural features. These k-mers were also used to develop a framework that enables the inference of haplogroups in a given sample based on short-read whole genome sequencing (WGS) data (ascairn). By applying ascairn to large-scale human population datasets ( n > 3,300), we revealed the diversity of aHOR-HGs and their geographic histories across populations. The rare k-mer-based approach was also applied to investigate the structure of 1p/19q co-deletion, a highly recurrent centromere-involving translocation in IDH -mutated oligodendrogliomas. Analyzing short-read WGS data from 142 cases with 1p/19q co-deletion using rare k-mers, we showed that breakpoints of 1p/19q co-deletion were mapped to aHOR arrays in chromosomes 1 ( D1Z7 ) and 19 ( D19Z3 ), which was validated by long-read sequencing of two 1p/19q co-deletion-positive cases. Notably, the translocation preferentially involved haplogroups composed of haplotypes containing larger regions susceptible to rearrangement. These results highlight the role of rare k-mers in dissecting the complexity of centromere sequences and their evolutionary history as well as understanding centromere-involving abnormalities associated with human diseases.

title: A high-dimensional population code in the bat motor cortex during natural dexterous flight
abstract: Elucidating the neural computations underlying natural, complex movement remains a fundamental challenge in neuroscience. Bat flight presents a formidable motor control challenge, requiring the use of hand-like wings whose many degrees of freedom must be precisely coordinated to enable rapid three-dimensional maneuvers. Here we performed large-scale wireless recordings of neuronal ensembles from the wing motor cortex of freely flying bats using Neuropixels probes, alongside detailed 3D pose tracking of wing kinematics. Despite the complexity of flight control, bats repeatedly executed highly accurate flights through precise adjustments of individual wingbeats. Surprisingly, motor cortical activity was not dominated by the global wingbeat cycle. Instead, individual neurons were sparsely active, exhibiting mixed selectivity for specific flight kinematics combined with variable entrainment to the wingbeat phase reaching millisecond-scale precision. This yielded a high-dimensional population regime driven by low shared variance across wingbeats, with successive wingbeats occupying distinct neural population states. Our findings reveal that during complex natural behavior the mammalian motor cortex operates in a high-dimensional computational regime that challenges prevailing views of motor cortical computation and underscores the importance of studying ethologically relevant behaviors to uncover neural principles governing brain function.

title: Mechanisms of transcription control by distal enhancers from single-gene nanoscopy
abstract: Distal enhancers activate genes over vast genomic distances, but how this communication occurs and what signals are transmitted are poorly understood. Using real-time single-gene nanoscopy and targeted perturbations, we define physical parameters and mechanisms of enhancer-promoter communication. We find that productive interactions are dynamic, occur at a proximity of ≲100 nm, and are coordinated with transcriptional bursts. Enhancers and promoters find one another not only through passive diffusion; we often directly observe them being actively brought together by cohesin-mediated loop extrusion, which is a key determinant of transcriptional burst frequency. We also discover that specific general transcription factors (GTFs) of RNA polymerase II machinery are key to initiating transcriptional bursts, and enhancer-promoter interactions activate bursting by embedding the promoter within GTF clusters that form at the enhancers. Our results resolve the molecular and biochemical signals involved in long-range gene activation and elucidate the biophysical mechanisms for their transmission from the enhancer to the promoter.

title: PTPRS mediates invasion of tetanus neurotoxin into the central nervous system
abstract: Tetanus neurotoxin (TeNT) invades the central nervous system (CNS) via retrograde transport through motoneurons. Whether a host factor is needed to mediate TeNT trafficking has remained unknown. Here, using pull-down and mass spectrometry analysis, and by developing a luciferase-based in vivo transport assay, we identify receptor protein tyrosine phosphatase sigma (PTPRS; PTPσ) as the retrograde transport receptor for TeNT. Global or motoneuron-specific PTPRS knockout (KO) abolishes TeNT entry into the CNS in mouse models. PTPRS-TeNT interactions occur in endosomes, prevent toxin translocation, and direct TeNT trafficking in neurons. Structural studies establish that the TeNT light chain and belt region bind to the immunoglobulin domain of PTPRS. Disrupting TeNT-PTPRS interactions blocks TeNT trafficking into the spinal cord; consistently, a PTPRS-binding-deficient TeNT mutant induces botulism-like flaccid paralysis. Thus, PTPRS is the host factor mediating TeNT trafficking into the CNS, revealing a targetable pathway for post-entry intervention and drug delivery into the CNS.

title: A pseudoenzyme sensor of trehalose-6-phosphate directly represses the metabolic integrator SnRK1 in plants
abstract: Trehalose-6-phosphate (T6P) is a central metabolic signal linking sugar availability to plant growth, carbon utilization, and productivity, yet its sensing and signaling mechanisms remain elusive. Using chemical biology and functional approaches, we identify the noncatalytic pseudoenzyme Class-II T6P synthase (TPS-II) as a T6P sensor in Arabidopsis. In the apo state, TPS-II dimerizes to form an autoinhibitory inter-subunit interaction. T6P binding to the N-terminal TPS-like domain triggers a conformational change that releases the C-terminal domain, enabling interaction with the central metabolic integrator SNF1-related protein kinase 1 (SnRK1) to repress its kinase activity. Loss of TPS-II genes activates catabolic and stress-responsive programs while suppressing anabolic gene expression, consistent with constitutive SnRK1 activity. Conservation of this T6P-TPS-II-SnRK1 signaling axis throughout the plant kingdom highlights its fundamental role in coupling carbon availability to metabolic homeostasis. These findings resolve a long-standing question in sugar signaling and provide a framework for improving crop carbon-use efficiency.

title: Sensing endoplasmic reticulum redox state by ethylene receptors
Multi-omics atlas of chronic exercise
abstract: Exercise reduces all-cause mortality, yet its molecular effects across organs, sexes, and circadian phases remain incompletely understood. We subjected mice to 8 weeks of voluntary wheel running and collected 22 tissues and plasma during active and inactive phases for bulk RNA sequencing, metabolomics, proteomics, and single-nucleus RNA and methylation sequencing. Exercise induced canonical fiber-type switching and widespread, tissue-specific remodeling, with the largest transcriptomic changes in skeletal muscle. Except for the hypothalamus, kidney, and lung, most tissues changed more during the active phase. Females showed broader transcriptional responses, with distinct downregulation. Pairing single-nucleus methylomes with transcriptomes resolved the cell types driving exercise-induced epigenetic remodeling-changes undetectable by bulk studies. These included coordinated gene-body demethylation and transcription that tracked with fiber-type switching in specific myonuclei. Cell-type-resolved methylation, including partially methylated domains characterized in muscle, revealed a strong, sex-biased epigenetic response to training. Machine learning identified conserved exercise signatures across mammalian species.

title: Cellular self-organization orchestrates ferroptosis propagation
abstract: Self-organization generates cellular patterns that guide morphogenesis, but how it regulates collective cell fate remains underexplored. We show that cellular self-organization constrains the propagation of ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of oxidative cell death that can otherwise spread as unbounded trigger waves. The spatial patterning of cell density and alignment encodes transcriptional programs, priming cells toward ferroptosis-sensitive or -resistant fates. Low-density, misaligned regions with elevated YAP/TEAD1 activity are sensitive, whereas high-density, aligned regions with increased NRF2 expression form propagation-resistant boundaries. Cell elongation establishes a polarized distribution of oxidizable lipids, creating peroxidation hotspots at the cell poles that promote propagation along cell alignment. In silico and pharmacological perturbations reveal that pattern-dependent susceptibility and polarized lipid organization act together to constrain isotropic waves into spatially confined, anisotropic propagation. These findings identify self-organization as a systems-level mechanism governing collective homeostasis, providing a paradigm to explore how tissue-scale organization regulates cell death in development and disease.

title: An opioid efficacy switch for reversible optical control of analgesia
abstract: The mu-opioid receptor (MOR) is a major target for pain treatment, but its effectiveness is limited by dangerous side effects. However, the systemic administration of opioids makes it difficult both to decipher their underlying mechanisms of action and to limit drug action to specific receptor subpopulations to isolate therapeutic effects from adverse effects. Here, we develop a reversibly photoswitchable morphinan agonist termed "azo-morphine-3" (AM-3) that interconverts from low to high efficacy in response to light to enable optical control of MOR signaling. Structural analysis of the low ("trans") and high ("cis") efficacy states of AM-3 bound to the MOR reveals distinct binding modes, with each state driving unique ligand, receptor, and G protein dynamics. In mice, AM-3 drives reversible and repeatable optical control of antinociception across pain models with a reduced side effect profile owing to its limited brain accumulation and its ability to be locally activated.

title: Functional diversification of the cephalopod proteome by RNA editing
abstract: Coleoid cephalopods exhibit the highest levels of adenosine deaminases acting on RNA (ADAR)-mediated RNA editing of any known taxon, yet the functional consequences of most recoding events remain unclear. Here, we integrated proteomics with biochemical and cellular assays to characterize recoding across the Doryteuthis pealeii proteome. This confirmed the translation of 7,997 recoded sites at the protein level and revealed how recoding reshapes the proteome by altering protein stability, subcellular localization, post-translational modifications, and enzymatic activity. We find that recoding also creates or ablates post-translational modification sites, with direct effects on protein function and protein-protein interactions. Recoding the E3 ligase MARCHF5 drives widespread changes in substrate ubiquitylation and perturbs mitochondrial homeostasis, illustrating how RNA editing can influence organelle function. Together, these data give a proteome-scale view of how extensive RNA recoding diversifies protein function in coleoid cephalopods and offer a framework for understanding how RNA-level plasticity shapes protein function and cellular physiology.

title: A phenome-wide structural variant map from 467,152 UK Biobank genomes
abstract: Structural variants (SVs) are large (>50 base pairs) genomic rearrangements that can significantly influence human phenotypes, yet their contribution to health and disease remains undercharacterized. We conducted a phenome-wide association study (PheWAS) of 1.6 million SVs identified in whole-genome sequencing data from 467,152 UK Biobank participants, across 13,322 binary, 2,018 quantitative, and 2,923 plasma protein traits. Of these, 82.25% of SVs were outside the detectable range of prior copy-number variant studies. Protein quantitative trait loci analysis linked 3,241 SVs to 1,608 proteins, with effects dependent on SV type and location. In SV-PheWAS, we detected 28,184 associations with human health outcomes. Notably, we uncovered rare SVs with strong phenotypic effects. Furthermore, we show that at known genome-wide association study loci, 32.21% of associated SVs overlapped functional genomic regions. This study underscores the underestimated role of SVs in human genetics and their potential to advance understanding of human biology and drug discovery.

title: Spatiotemporal co-transcriptomics uncovers coordinated rhizobia-legume stress programs supporting nitrogen fixation in Medicago
abstract: Rhizobial nitrogen fixation in legume nodules requires precise spatial and temporal coordination between host and bacterial gene expression. Here, we applied spatial enhanced resolution omics sequencing (Stereo-seq) to profile Medicago nodules across five developmental stages, generating a co-transcriptomic atlas of nodule development. Using a mixed-probe capture strategy, we simultaneously detected host and rhizobial transcripts within the same tissue sections, enabling analysis of host-microbe transcriptional coordination during symbiosis. We identified dynamic changes in host cell composition and developmental trajectories and uncovered two transcription factors, MtERF82 and MtDOF53, required for maintenance of the indeterminate nodule meristem. Rhizobial and host genes exhibited stage- and zone-specific expression patterns along the nodule apex-to-base axis. Notably, reactive oxygen species (ROS)-associated stress responses in both host cells and rhizobia were linked to symbiotic nitrogen fixation. Functional analyses further showed that MtERF71 and MtCBF1 promote nitrogen fixation by regulating ROS homeostasis and activating key symbiotic genes, highlighting stress signaling as an integral component of mutualistic symbiosis.

title: Cellular scaling laws in the mammalian brain
abstract: Recent whole-brain cell atlases have uncovered a consistent cytoarchitectural feature: the greatest diversity of discrete neuronal cell types resides not in the regions with the most neurons (e.g., the cortex and cerebellum) but rather in deep subcortical structures like the hypothalamus and brain stem. We propose that this discrepancy reflects a fundamental algorithmic division in the vertebrate brain between a "learning subsystem" and a "steering subsystem." The learning subsystem (cortex, striatum, and cerebellum) scales via the replication of repetitive modules to maximize computational capacity, analogous to scaling up parameters in machine learning models. By contrast, the steering subsystem (hypothalamus, pallidum, and brainstem) scales via diversification of bespoke cell types to encode innate drives and reflexes, functioning as a high-dimensional biological "reward function." This framework explains the divergence in how evolution has influenced these subsystems and offers a unified lens for understanding brain architecture and the etiology of brain disease; furthermore, it may inform model designs for artificial intelligence.

title: Milking the niche: Microbial control of neonatal hematopoiesis
abstract: In this issue of Cell, Howard et al. reveal how the milk glycoprotein osteopontin shapes the neonatal microbiome to regulate hematopoiesis, promoting dendritic cell development and protection from severe respiratory infection. These findings uncover a maternal milk-microbiota pathway linking early-life nutrition to immune development and long-term disease susceptibility.

title: A telomere-to-telomere map of somatic mutation burden and functional impact in a cancer
abstract: Cancer genomes harbor extensive somatic genetic and epigenetic variation, yet large portions of the genome remain inaccessible to conventional reference-based analyses. Here, we demonstrate that pairing a near-telomere-to-telomere (near-T2T) diploid assembly of a donor with deep short- and long-read sequencing of their melanoma reveals that 16% of somatic variants localize to sequences absent from GRCh38, with satellite repeats acting as hotspots for UV-associated mutagenesis. Centromere kinetochore binding domains emerge as focal sites of chromosome arm aneuploidy breakpoints and somatic genetic variation, features we further demonstrate are also present in non-cancerous tissues. By contrast, extensive epigenetic remodeling of kinetochore binding domains appears specific to oncogenesis. Single-molecule telomere analyses reconstruct the cycle of telomere erosion and telomerase-mediated extension during tumor evolution, while haplotype-resolved chromatin maps reveal widespread somatic epimutations impacting regulatory elements. Together, these findings define previously inaccessible dimensions of somatic variation and establish a framework for telomere-to-telomere studies of human mosaicism.

title: Somatic epimutations cap genetic determinism in the human diploid chromatin epigenome
abstract: Diploid human cells contain two non-identical genomes, and differences in their regulation underlie human development and disease. We present Fiber-seq Inferred Regulatory Elements (FIRE) and show that FIRE provides a more comprehensive and quantitative snapshot of the accessible chromatin landscape across the 6 Gbp diploid human genome, overcoming previously known and unknown biases afflicting our existing regulatory element catalog. FIRE provides a comprehensive genome-wide map of haplotype-selective chromatin accessibility (HSCA), exposing novel imprinted elements that lack underlying parent-of-origin CpG methylation differences, common and rare genetic variants that disrupt gene regulatory patterns, gene regulatory modules that enable genes to escape X chromosome inactivation, and autosomal mitotically stable somatic epimutations. We find that the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) locus harbors the most HSCA in immune cells, and we resolve the specific transcription factor (TF) binding events disrupted by disease-associated variants within the HLA locus. Finally, we demonstrate that the regulatory landscape of a cell is littered with autosomal somatic epimutations that are propagated by clonal expansions to create mitotically stable and non-genetically deterministic chromatin alterations.

title: Comprehensive benchmarking of somatic mutation detection by the SMaHT Network
abstract: Somatic mosaicism is increasingly recognized as a fundamental feature of human biology, yet the detection of somatic mutations remains challenging. The Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues (SMaHT) Network conducted large-scale benchmarking experiments involving cell lines and donor tissues to evaluate sequencing technologies, experimental approaches, and computational methods for detecting different types of somatic mutations, generating community resources with >1,000× short-read and 100-400× long-read data for nine analyzed samples. We determined effective strategies for utilizing short- and long-read sequencing for mutation detection and demonstrated that using donor-specific and pangenome-inferred diploid assemblies improved calling, extending mutation catalogs to challenging genomic regions. We benchmarked six duplex technologies and showed that single-cell sequencing resolves cell-type-specific mutational patterns and heterogeneity. Our results indicate that bulk, single-cell, and duplex analyses are complementary and that leveraging all three provides comprehensive characterization of mosaicism within tissues. Together, these findings provide the scientific and clinical communities with a roadmap for accurate genome-wide somatic mutation analysis.

title: Charting the silent variation within us
abstract: Every cell in the human body carries its own genome, shaped by mutations acquired over a lifetime, yet this vast somatic variation has been nearly impossible to measure. The SMaHT Network now delivers benchmarked tools and the first body-wide map of somatic mosaicism, establishing a baseline of "normal" against which its roles in development, aging, and disease can finally be tested.

title: Mitochondria-targeted tetraoxanes initiate lipid peroxidation to drive ferroptosis and tumor suppression
abstract: Ferroptosis is implicated as a vulnerability in multiple cancers, yet approaches for effectively inducing ferroptosis in vivo are limited. Bypassing conventional strategies targeting the antiferroptotic glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) and ferroptosis suppressor protein 1 (FSP1) proteins, we designed metabolic initiators of lipid peroxidation (MILPOs) and developed the compounds WMK-1/2, which contain tetraoxane radical-generating and mitochondria-targeting groups, as de novo ferroptosis inducers. WMK-1 localizes primarily to mitochondria, induces local lipid peroxidation, and impairs oxidative phosphorylation. WMK-1 induces a "mito-ferroptosis" sub-pathway that skips GPX4 inhibition as a prerequisite, can be rescued by lipophilic radical-trapping antioxidants, yet is minimally sensitive to acyl-coenzyme A synthetase long-chain family member 4 (ACSL4) perturbation and long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) supplementation, and evades retinol-mediated protection. Instead, WMK-1-induced cell death requires labile Fe 2+ and can be selectively suppressed by ɑ-lipoic acid, an endogenous, mitochondria-resident antioxidant. WMK-1/2 are bioavailable and exhibit significant efficacy in tumor suppression by eliciting ferroptosis in multiple cancer models and augmenting the antitumor effects of immune-checkpoint blockers. Our work provides a protein-targeting-independent metabolic ferroptosis induction strategy for potential cancer therapy.

title: A microbiome-bile acid axis mediates protection from chronic liver disease in females
abstract: Sex-based differences in chronic liver disease (CLD) incidence and progression are well documented, yet the mechanistic basis of this sexual disparity remains elusive. Here, leveraging a large-scale metabolomics database comprising 9,254 individuals, we identify the endogenous bile acid, isoursodeoxycholic acid (isoUDCA), as a candidate mediator of female-associated hepatoprotection. We trace the origin of isoUDCA to a bacterial consortium, which is selectively enriched by estrogen through shaping a specialized intestinal microenvironment. Mechanistically, isoUDCA promotes the nuclear accumulation of SREBP2. This upregulates the intracellular transporter STARD4 and its functionally coupled downstream enzyme CYP7B1, thereby facilitating intracellular cholesterol handling and metabolic conversion. Collectively, our findings support a microbiome-bile acid-liver axis that may contribute to sex differences in CLD susceptibility and support further evaluation of isoUDCA as a potential therapeutic intervention.

title: The pyrin inflammasome senses OCTN2-mediated uptake of extracellular ʟ-carnitine from muscle injury or ingestion
abstract: Red-meat-containing diets are epidemiologically associated with diseases of chronic inflammation, while diets that restrict red meat improve health. Yet, it is uncertain how red meat incites inflammation. Here, we discover that ʟ-carnitine, an amino acid highly concentrated in skeletal muscle myocytes, drives inflammasome activation in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-challenged mice and LPS-primed murine and human macrophages. We find that extracellular ʟ-carnitine represses mevalonate synthesis, thereby triggering activation of the pyrin inflammasome, downstream of cellular import by the high-affinity ʟ-carnitine transporter OCTN2. We find that the inflammatory response to skeletal muscle injury also requires pyrin and OCTN2. Thus, in summary, we identify macrophages as sentinels of exogenous and endogenous extracellular ʟ-carnitine that serve as a proxy for skeletal myocyte damage, and we open the field to examine the mechanistic basis for how excess dietary intake of carnitine-rich food drives inflammatory disease.

title: Structural basis of a SWI/SNF-associated transcription pre-initiation complex
Root microbiota regulates tiller number in rice
Promoter of lncRNA Gene PVT1 Is a Tumor-Suppressor DNA Boundary Element
Contrasting demographic impacts of Roman colonization and early medieval migrations in the Iberian Peninsula
abstract: It has been unclear how Roman and later Germanic political control shaped the demography of Iberia and how it differed from other parts of Europe. We report genetic data from 243 ancient individuals dating to 100-800 CE, analyzed alongside 58 previously published individuals. In Roman times, we document an influx of people with ancestry from the Eastern Mediterranean and an influx of North Africans, especially in the center and south. Beginning in the 5th century, Germanic and Alan (Sarmatian) groups assumed political control. Although we identify individuals with Central-Northern European-associated ancestry, including siblings buried ∼725 km apart, the Hispano-Roman population remained continuous in Iberia. These demographic patterns contrast sharply with those in Britain, where major demographic change followed Rome's collapse, and with those in the central Mediterranean, where both periods were associated with profound transformations. Together, these findings highlight regional variation in admixture and continuity across post-Roman Europe.

title: In vivo Gene Writing with engineered retrotransposons
abstract: Efficient integration of gene-length cargos in vivo remains challenging. Non-long terminal repeat (non-LTR) retrotransposons, which naturally mobilize large DNA segments through an RNA intermediate, could potentially address these limitations. Here, we developed a computational pipeline to systematically identify a diverse set of non-LTR retrotransposons. Extensive engineering generated elements capable of the efficient and stable insertion of reporter genes in human cells using RNA templates introduced in trans, which we term Gene Writers. Gene Writers successfully generated CD19 and CD20 chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cells ex vivo with robust antitumor activity. Lipid nanoparticle-mediated RNA delivery enabled in vivo CAR-T cell generation and stable B cell depletion in a humanized mouse model. Our study delineates a comprehensive framework for the discovery, engineering, and application of non-LTR retrotransposons and demonstrates their utility for gene-sized cargo delivery in vivo, thereby bridging a critical gap in existing gene therapy modalities.

title: Proteomic atlas of T cell exhaustion defines proteostatic collapse
abstract: T cell exhaustion limits the success of cancer immunotherapies, yet the proteomic changes underlying this dysfunctional state remain poorly understood. We integrated transcriptomics, quantitative proteomics, turnover proteomics, and ubiquitin proteomics to construct a multi-omic atlas of T cell exhaustion. These studies identified pathways regulated through transcriptional and post-translational mechanisms, including degradative and nondegradative ubiquitin modifications, and uncovered widespread changes in proteostasis, metabolism, and DNA repair. Major shifts were revealed in the ubiquitin-proteasome system, as differential expression of E3 ubiquitin ligases correlates with immunotherapy outcomes. These findings position the collapse of proteostasis as a central, underappreciated feature of T cell exhaustion and reveal opportunities to restore T cell function. We demonstrate that overexpression of the E3 ligase RNF166 enhances T cell persistence in vitro and in vivo. This work defines proteome-turnover dynamics as a critical regulatory layer in progressive T cell dysfunction, with broad implications for advancing cancer immunotherapy through manipulation of E3 ligases.

title: A bioavailable GPX4 inhibitor for ferroptosis induction in vivo and tumor suppression
abstract: Ferroptosis is implicated in multiple human diseases, but the lack of bioavailable inducers has limited its physiological study and therapeutic translation. Here, we report KY0418, a selective covalent inhibitor of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) featuring an isourea warhead, with high plasma stability and broad tissue distribution after oral dosing in mice. KY0418 specifically targets GPX4 SeCys46 to induce ferroptosis hallmarks in human and mouse cancer cell lines, with greater selectivity than existing inhibitors. In a standardizable acute-liver-injury mouse model, KY0418 triggers ferroptotic ultrastructural changes matching those of established inducers, and systemic administration remodels tissue metabolism and generates hydroxyl radicals detectable by a chemiluminescent probe. Subcutaneous tumors from different cancers exhibited variable responses to KY0418 treatment, from no effect to about 70% growth inhibition, but KY0418 consistently eradicated circulating tumor cells and suppressed metastasis across multiple cancer models. These findings position KY0418 as a tool for advancing in vivo ferroptosis research and its clinical translation.

title: Lifestyle-induced regulatory T cell fragility primes adverse events after immune checkpoint blockade
abstract: Immune checkpoint blockade has transformed cancer therapy, but immune-related adverse events (irAEs) remain a major, sometimes fatal, limitation, and the lack of robust preclinical models has hindered mechanistic insight. We present the lifestyle-induced susceptibility to irAEs (LISA) model, in which diet-driven metabolic and microbial alterations recreate human-like susceptibility to anti-PD-1 toxicity. LISA recapitulates multi-organ irAEs with immune infiltration and cytokine production, severity depending on sex, age, treatment modality, and immunotherapy response. Mechanistically, dysbiosis marked by Akkermansia muciniphila enrichment accompanies aberrant immune activation, driving regulatory T cell (Treg) fragility and CD8 + cytotoxic effector populations, both observed in patients with irColitis. Dietary reversal, metabolite supplementation, and blocking interferon (IFN)-γ production or signaling in Tregs restored Treg stability and resolved inflammation. Human-to-mouse fecal microbiome transfer interacts with recipient diet to shape susceptibility. Together, these findings identify dietary, microbial, and immune drivers of irAEs, which can be leveraged to improve immunotherapy responses while minimizing toxicity.

title: Metazoan lagging-strand DNA synthesis is distributive
abstract: DNA's anti-parallel structure presents a topological challenge to the replisome, as leading and lagging strands must be synthesized in opposite directions. How lagging-strand synthesis is coordinated with leading-strand synthesis remains unresolved in eukaryotes. To address this question, we directly visualized the dynamics of lagging-strand polymerases Pol α and Pol δ at active replication forks using single-molecule imaging in Xenopus nuclear extracts. Surprisingly, we find that neither Pol α nor Pol δ is stably tethered to the replisome. Instead, lagging-strand synthesis occurs distributively and entails the rapid recruitment of new molecules of Pol α and Pol δ for each Okazaki fragment. Consequently, leading- and lagging-strand synthesis are not intrinsically coupled. We propose that metazoans solve the problem of anti-parallel replication not by actively coordinating leading- and lagging-strand synthesis, but instead simply by recruiting new polymerases to synthesize each Okazaki fragment.

title: MCT6 is an intestinal Lac-Phe exporter required for metformin-associated weight loss
abstract: Metabolites are increasingly recognized as circulating molecules that regulate physiology, yet the mechanisms that couple intracellular production to organism-wide action remain poorly defined. Using the anorexigenic metabolite Lac-Phe as a tractable system, we identify the orphan transporter MCT6 (SLC16A5) as a physiologic intestinal Lac-Phe exporter. This mechanism controls the extent to which intracellularly synthesized Lac-Phe acquires systemic activity. MCT6 transports Lac-Phe, mediates its cellular efflux, and is required for maintaining its blood levels in mice following strong glycolytic stimuli. Both global and intestinal epithelial-specific deletion of MCT6 confers resistance to metformin-associated weight loss on a high-fat diet. Bypassing the transport defect with exogenous Lac-Phe normalizes the body weight phenotype of MCT6-KO mice. Together, these data connect MCT6 to metformin pharmacology and intestinal lactate metabolism, and more generally underscore the importance of transporter-mediated release in the conversion of an intracellular metabolic state into a circulating metabolite effector.

title: Cell-state-specific metabolic networks govern ferroptosis versus apoptosis in small cell lung cancer
abstract: Cellular heterogeneity and plasticity are hallmarks of cancer that contribute to tumor growth and therapy resistance. Here, we investigated metabolic heterogeneity in small cell lung cancer (SCLC), an aggressive cancer type with considerable plasticity between neuroendocrine (NE) and non-NE cellular states. Through integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses, we identified a universal dependency on exogenous cysteine/cystine (Cys) across all NE/non-NE SCLC cell states. Notably, NE and non-NE cells with low ASCL1 transcription factor levels underwent ferroptosis upon Cys depletion, whereas ASCL1 high cells underwent apoptosis while remaining resistant to ferroptosis. This ferroptosis resistance was driven by the direct transcriptional activation of GCH1 by ASCL1, resulting in increased levels of the antioxidants BH4/BH2. Accordingly, combined Cys depletion and inhibition of BH4/BH2 synthesis reduced tumor growth in patient-derived xenografts. These findings demonstrate that metabolic state influences cell-death susceptibility in SCLC and provide a rationale for therapeutic strategies that exploit these metabolic differences.

title: Taurine lowers inflammaging by regulating the NLRP3 inflammasome in macrophages
abstract: Abstract Taurine, the most abundant sulfonic amino acid in humans is largely obtained from diets rich in animal proteins. However, taurine is dietary non-essential because it can be synthesized from cysteine by activation of transsulfuration pathway (TSP) when food consumption is low or if the diet is predominantly plant based. The decline of taurine was proposed as the driver of aging through an undefined mechanism. Here, we found that mild food restriction in humans for one year that resulted in 14% reduction of calorie intake elevated the hypotaurine and taurine concentration in adipose tissue. Therefore, we investigated whether elevated taurine mimics caloric-restriction’s beneficial effects on inflammation, a key mechanism of aging. Interestingly, aging increased the circulating and tissue concentrations of taurine suggesting that elevated taurine may serve as a hormetic stress response metabolite that regulates mechanism of age-related inflammation. The elevated taurine protected mice against mortality from sepsis and inhibited inflammasome-driven inflammation and gasdermin-D (GSDMD) mediated pyroptosis. Mechanistically, ‘danger signals’ including hypotonicity that activate NLRP3-inflammasome, caused upstream taurine efflux from macrophages, which triggered potassium (K + ) release and downstream canonical NLRP3 inflammasome assembly, caspase-1 activation, GSDMD cleavage and IL-1β and IL-18 secretion that was reversed by taurine restoration. Notably, taurine does not efflux from GSDMD pore and inhibited IL-1β from macrophages independently of known transporters SLC6A6 and SLC36A1. Increased taurine in old mice promotes healthspan by inducing anti-inflammatory pathways previously linked to youthfulness. These findings demonstrate that taurine is an upstream metabolic sensor of cellular perturbations that control NLRP3 inflammasome and lowers age-related inflammation.

title: Perforin triggers iron-induced mitochondrial damage to drive ferroptosis and anti-tumor immunity
abstract: T cells and natural killer cells are critical effectors of anti-tumor immunity. Cytotoxic lymphocytes eliminate tumor cells by releasing perforin (Prf1), a pore-forming protein that enables granzymes (Gzms) to enter target cells and trigger both caspase-dependent and -independent cell death. Here, we uncover a previously unrecognized, Gzm-independent function of Prf1. We find that Prf1 directly induces tumoral ferroptosis, an iron- and lipid-dependent form of cell death. Mechanistically, Prf1-mediated pore formation drives endocytosis of the transferrin receptor, which increases cellular iron uptake. Prf1 promotes the formation of endosomal-mitochondrial contacts, which leads to mitochondrial iron accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and tumor cell ferroptosis. Dietary iron supplementation suppresses tumor progression in murine tumor models in a Prf1-dependent manner. Higher Prf1 expression correlates with improved survival and enhanced response to immune checkpoint blockade in patients with cancer. These findings define a Gzm-independent function of Prf1 as a direct executioner of cancer cell death through ferroptosis.

title: In vivo genome-editing therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy: Preclinical studies and first-in-human trial
abstract: We report the preclinical and early clinical evaluation of in vivo genome editing for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), delivered via a single AAV9 vector. In humanized DMD mice, systemic administration achieved targeted genome editing, partial dystrophin restoration, and improved muscle function. In non-human primates, efficient on-target editing was achieved with no dose-limiting toxicity identified under the conditions tested. In an open-label, dose-escalation, first-in-human clinical trial (NCT06594094), post-treatment muscle biopsies provided early molecular evidence of hfCas12Max-mediated genome editing and detectable dystrophin expression in participants with DMD. However, at the higher dose level (1.0 × 10 14 vg/kg), one participant experienced a treatment-related fatal serious adverse event, characterized by marked complement activation and systemic cytokine response shortly after dosing. This work provides initial human proof-of-concept for muscle genome editing while crucially highlighting the critical role of immunologic risks and the narrow therapeutic window of systemic adeno-associated virus (AAV)-CRISPR therapies, underscoring the need to develop safer dosing and immunomodulation strategies.

title: Deep sequencing of 3,367 maize genomes uncovers substantial contribution of rare variants to agronomic traits
abstract: Rare variants are highly abundant, yet their genome-wide contributions to agronomic traits remain elusive in plants. Here, we performed deep whole-genome sequencing of 3,367 diverse elite maize inbred lines, uncovering 75.3 million variants, of which 79.2% were rare. Overall, we identified 411 independent association signals for 10 agronomic traits, including 359 attributable to globally rare variants, with rare variants showing effect sizes approximately 2.4 times those of common variants. Frequency-stratified genome-based restricted maximum likelihood (GREML) analyses indicated that rare variants captured a substantial proportion of phenotypic variance for traits under strong adaptive selection, consistent with the allele frequencies of trait-associated variants shifting from common in tropical to rare in temperate maize. Complementing conventional variant-level genome-wide association studies (GWAS), gene-based tests identified an additional 94 candidate gene-trait associations. Our study highlights rare variants as important components of the genetic architecture of complex agronomic traits in maize and provides much-needed resources for future functional studies and breeding.

title: Long-range actin-driven endosymbiont mobility in an animal-algal symbiosis
abstract: In animal-microbe symbioses, established symbionts are often thought to be confined to a niche and to lose motile appendages such as flagella. Whether this loss implies immobility within the host remains poorly understood. We report long-range, host-driven symbiont mobility in a dinoflagellate-acoel worm symbiosis. Using long-term tracking, fluorescence, and electron microscopy, we find that hundreds of dinoflagellate symbionts (Amphidinium sp., 10-20 μm in size) travel across the body of an acoel worm host (Waminoa sp.) at around 1 μm/s while confined inside a network of ultra-thin (∼200 nm) host parenchymal cells. We show this mobility is driven by host actin machinery, with symbionts moving faster than comparable actin-based transport systems despite confinement. We further show spatiotemporal regulation of symbiont distribution during diel rhythms and regeneration. By characterizing an active, host-cytoskeleton-driven mechanism of symbiont transport, our work expands our understanding of the regulatory strategies by which holobionts maintain dynamic homeostasis.

title: Somatic DNA-repeat expansions initiate distinct yet analogous changes in Huntington’s disease cortical and striatal neurons
abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) affects the neocortex and striatum with different timing, severity, and gene-expression changes. These pathologies have long been proposed to involve different pathogenic mechanisms, with one brain area's degeneration leading to the other's. Striatal neurons degenerate in HD as their huntingtin (HTT) CAG-repeat tracts expand somatically beyond 150 CAGs. Here, we find that cortical pyramidal neurons in HD undergo biological changes analogous to those in striatal neurons-the same sequence of pathological phases, with toxicity also commencing at ∼150 CAGs but then changing their gene expression in distinct ways. Pyramidal neurons' precise molecular identities, rather than their areal or laminar locations, appeared to determine the extent of this somatic DNA-repeat expansion, which varied up to 20-fold among pyramidal neuron subtypes. Cortical and striatal neurons also shared a key pathological feature: nuclear inclusions of aggregated HTT protein in those nuclei with expansions well beyond 150 CAGs.

title: Multimodal spatial transcriptomics redefines cortical pathology in Huntington’s disease
abstract: ABSTRACT Huntington’s disease (HD) is caused by CAG expansion in HTT , yet how somatic repeat instability and huntingtin aggregation relate to selective cell loss in the human brain remains unclear. We have developed a multimodal spatial transcriptomics approach that enables defining transcriptional programs with subcellular resolution, somatic CAG repeat lengths, and six other pathology marks including huntingtin aggregates in every cell of intact brain sections. Imaging 428,173 cells in HD cortex revealed selective vulnerability: L5–6 NP and L6b deep-layer excitatory neurons undergo >50% loss, closely linked to very large (>380±55) somatic expansions. Intranuclear aggregation was most prevalent at intermediate somatic repeat expansion (220-300 CAGs) and was accompanied by broader transcriptional changes. In contrast, chandelier and somatostatin+ inhibitory interneurons are lost despite only modest repeat expansion or aggregation. These data provide a comprehensive resource and establish a broadly applicable framework for connecting repeat expansion and protein pathology across diverse cell types. Short Bullet points Development of a novel, multimodal spatial transcriptomics platform enables definition of RNA transcriptomes with subcellular resolution, somatic repeat expansions, and protein accumulation in cells within tissue sections Generation of two complementary datasets for HD and control cortex: 428,173 cells to quantify comprehensively cell-type vulnerability, and a deeper multimodal dataset in which CAG repeat expansion, huntingtin aggregation, six additional pathological readouts, and expression of 1,128 genes were measured in 185,721 cells, providing a comprehensive resource for the neurodegeneration community. Deep layer excitatory neuron loss (L5–6 NP and L6b) was associated with very large somatic CAG expansions (>380±55), while selective inhibitory neuron loss (chandelier and somatostatin interneurons) occurred with modest CAG repeat expansion or huntingtin intranuclear aggregation Intranuclear aggregation, not somatic repeat expansion, was more predictive of transcriptional changes, including chromatin remodeling and RNA export factors

title: Innate sensor responses set a supra-unitary threshold for viral replication
abstract: Cells resist viral infection by triggering rapid and sensitive innate immune responses, initiated by cytoplasmic viral sensor proteins (CyVSP), retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I), melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5 (MDA-5), and protein kinase R (PKR). Our single-cell analysis reveals that viral replication requires a supra-unitary viral genome input, significantly more than one, which we define as the virion input threshold for replication (VITREP). This threshold varies depending on viruses and cell types, independently of viral protein synthesis. Through mathematical modeling and experimental testing, we uncover that supra-unitary viral genome quantities activate negative feedback regulators (NFR) of CyVSP, including death-associated protein kinase 1 (DAPK1), Rio kinase 3 (RIOK3), and protein phosphatase 2 regulatory subunit alpha (PPP2R2A), that suppress innate immune responses and allow replication. We validate key predictions of our model, namely that downregulating NFR reduces replication, whereas upregulating NFR or coinfecting cells promotes replication. Together, these findings reveal a fundamental mechanism governing viral infectivity and tissue tropism.

title: Genetic coupling of floral rewards and signals underlies pollinator attraction
abstract: Animal pollinators underpin biodiversity and global agriculture, yet the molecular mechanisms that coordinate floral rewards and signals to attract pollinators remain poorly understood. Through phenotyping melon genetic diversity, we identified nectarless1 (nls1), encoding the YABBY-family transcription factor YABBY5 (YAB5), as a central integrator of pollinator-attracting traits. YAB5 interacts with CRABS CLAW (CRC) during nectary initiation to specify nectary identity by repressing alternative floral organ fates. As flowers mature, YAB5 directly activates 4-α-glucanotransferase 2 (DPE2) to promote starch remobilization required for nectar secretion and promotes petal growth and flower opening. In petals, YAB5 directly engages an MYB111-dependent flavonoid pathway that generates UV nectar guides, while indirectly influencing floral volatile emission. Disrupting YAB5, DPE2, or MYB111 reduces pollinator visitation. Together, these findings reveal how a developmental regulator couples organ specification with organ-specific metabolic programs to synchronize floral rewards and signals at anthesis.

title: Roads not taken: The mismatch between safety and regulation of plant breeding innovation
abstract: Meeting global food security goals while reducing agriculture's environmental impact requires continued crop improvement and innovation. Advances in transgenesis, cisgenesis, and genome editing now enable increasingly precise genetic modification with risks comparable to those of conventional breeding, yet regulatory frameworks remain focused on the method used rather than the product. We highlight recent examples, including immune receptor transfer, cisgenesis-based disease resistance stacking, photosynthesis engineering, and AI-guided protein design, that illustrate innovations constrained by current regulatory approaches. A decisive shift toward science-based, proportionate, and product-focused regulation is needed so that improved crops are evaluated on the basis of their properties, not how they were made.

title: Toward planetary microbial systems biology
abstract: Microorganisms underpin Earth's biosphere, sustaining life, shaping biogeochemical cycles, and maintaining ecosystem stability. In an era of scientific and geopolitical fragmentation, we advocate for a "planetary microbial systems biology" (PMSB) framework to uncover the mechanisms and organizational principles governing Earth's interconnected microbial systems across scales of matter, space, and time and in relation to underlying natural and anthropogenic drivers. PMSB combines molecular and cellular technologies, multi-omics data, artificial intelligence (AI), and integrated transdisciplinary research across ecosystems. By federating open data and combining field observations, experimentation, and modeling, PMSB enables predictive understanding of microbiome dynamics across planetary scales, thus filling a critical knowledge gap in our understanding of the co-evolution of life and the Earth-system.

title: Calorie restriction uncouples mutation rate from lifespan
abstract: In this issue of Cell, Grońska-Pęski et al. examine how calorie restriction (CR) affects DNA mutation rates. While CR lowers the accumulation of mutations, this effect does not scale with the degree of lifespan extension. Their work raises important new questions about how CR impacts the causal mechanisms of aging.

title: Guardians at the gate: cMAF keeps the brain’s vasculature in check
abstract: In this issue of Cell, Brioschi et al. identify cellular musculoaponeurotic fibrosarcoma (cMAF) as a key regulator of brain perivascular macrophages that supports cerebrovascular function through insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) production. This cMAF-IGF1 program is enhanced in Alzheimer's disease (AD), potentially reflecting a protective response that is lost in APOE4 carriers.

title: Age-dependent structural evolution of a functional amyloid contributes to memory impairment in Drosophila
abstract: Cryogenic electron microscopy has revealed endpoint structures of ex vivo amyloid filaments, but how amyloids assemble and evolve in living organisms-and how these transitions affect physiology-remains poorly understood. Here, we map the age-dependent structural landscape of Orb2 amyloid, a synaptic translation regulator required for long-term memory, across the adult lifespan of Drosophila melanogaster. By determining multiple Orb2 amyloid structures, we uncover a dynamic, age-linked progression of amyloid states. Translation-promoting assemblies predominate early in life, whereas aging shifts the Orb2 amyloid ensemble toward structurally distinct, destabilization-resistant assemblies with reduced translational activity, coinciding with memory impairment. Manipulating memory-related chaperones in the brain shifts Orb2 toward youthful, translation-promoting states and improves memory in old flies; conversely, shifting Orb2 toward aged-like, translation-deficient states in young adults is associated with premature memory impairment. These findings define an in vivo trajectory of amyloid evolution and link amyloid structural dynamics to synaptic translation and memory.

title: Fatty acid desaturation controls cellular fate decisions between senescence and ferroptosis
abstract: When subject to damage or stress, cells develop responses in order to maintain tissue homeostasis. Two such responses are ferroptosis and cellular senescence, but how cells decide between these outcomes remains unclear. Here, we show that senescent cells increase import and membrane levels of multiple polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), but a specific intermediate PUFA, dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid (DGLA, 20:3ω-6), is reduced. Exogenous repletion of DGLA instead results in cell death by ferroptosis. Senescent cells manifest additional features associated with ferroptosis, including labile iron and expression of lipoxygenases as well as low-level membrane peroxidation. Oral DGLA supplementation lowers markers of senescence in aged mice and improves age-related functional outcomes. Finally, obese humans with lowered DGLA desaturation rates have lower markers of adipose tissue senescence. Together, our data implicate shifts in PUFA metabolism as a driver of decisions between senescence and ferroptosis.

title: Subsistence transition preceded population turnover in the eastern Colombian Andes
abstract: The Altiplano Cundiboyacense in the eastern Colombian Andes preserves one of the Americas' most continuous archaeological sequences, recording cultural and demographic change. We generated genome-wide data from 212 individuals spanning over 7,000 years, including early-middle and middle Holocene hunter-gatherers, initial late Holocene groups with mixed economies and the earliest isotopic evidence of maize consumption, and increasingly sedentary Herrera and Muisca populations. Individuals predating the Herrera Period form a lineage that persisted for five millennia, structured by drift in small groups without external gene flow. Two individuals dating ∼2,800 years before present (BP) retain autochthonous ancestry while showing isotopic signatures consistent with maize consumption, decoupling subsistence change from population replacement. The emergence of Herrera culture ∼2,200 BP coincided with a sharp genetic break by ∼2,000 BP, which reflects migration by people descended from admixture ∼4,000 BP between groups with Chibchan- and Amazonian-Andean-related ancestries. Herrera and Muisca Period individuals show north-south genetic substructure paralleling archaeological differentiation.

title: Convergent genomic evolution of human gut bacteria along an industrialization gradient
abstract: To what extent gut bacteria respond to the distinct ecological pressures imposed by human lifestyle remains unclear. Here, we investigate how genomic adaptation in gut bacteria differ between industrialized and non-industrialized human populations. We generated a broad collection of isolate genomes spanning diverse host geographies, lifestyles, species, and strains. We first found that compared to MAGs, paired isolate genomes recover more functional elements and signals of horizontal gene transfers (HGTs). Leveraging isolate genomes from multiple species, we find that strains from industrialized hosts experience an expansion of proteome size and harbor greater pangenome fluidity, driven by recent events of HGTs. Gene- and variant-level analyses reveal convergent patterns of lifestyle-specific adaptation in functions that are critical for ecological adaptation, such as stress response, cell envelope remodeling and central metabolism. Our results demonstrate that industrialization imprints evolutionary signatures on gut bacterial genomes, illuminating the effects of rapidly changing environments on human biology.

title: Industrialization drives convergent microbiome and host physiological shifts in the human metaorganism
abstract: Understanding how host lifestyle and industrialization shape the human gut microbiome and intestinal physiology requires multimodal analyses across diverse global host contexts. Here, we generate multivariate data from the Global Microbiome Conservancy cohort, including gut microbiome, IgA-sequencing, host genotyping, diet, lifestyle and fecal biomarker profiles, to investigate host-microbiome interactions across gradients of industrialization and geography. We show that industrialization is associated with homogenized microbial compositions, reduced microbial diversity, and lower community stability, independent of host confounders. We further show that industrialization is linked to elevated markers of gut stress, increased IgA secretion, and altered patterns of IgA-bacteria interactions. Finally, we show that microbiome-based disease predictors trained on industrialized populations lose accuracy in less industrialized cohorts, highlighting limited cross-population transferability. Together, our results suggest profound restructuring of host-microbiome interactions due to industrialized lifestyles, and emphasize the need for inclusive, globally representative data to improve translational microbiome applications across diverse human populations.

title: TECR palmitoylation triggers a necrotic cell death program driving acute liver injury
abstract: Acute liver injury caused by drug toxicity or immune activation remains a major clinical challenge with limited mechanistic understanding and few effective therapies. Here, we identify a previously unrecognized form of regulated cell death driven by palmitoylation of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-resident enzyme trans-2,3-enoyl-coenzyme A (CoA) reductase (TECR). We show that multi-site palmitoylation of TECR, redundantly catalyzed by the palmitoyl acyltransferases ZDHHC5 and ZDHHC2 and dynamically reversed by the depalmitoylase ABHD10, activates PERK-dependent ER stress signaling to trigger cell death. This cell death pathway is a TECR-dependent, palmitoylation-induced, ER stress-mediated necrotic cell death program (TPNCD). TPNCD contributes to liver injury in mouse models of acetaminophen- and concanavalin A-induced hepatotoxicity and is attenuated by hepatocyte-specific TECR ablation or by pharmacological inhibition of palmitoylation or ER stress signaling. Together, these findings establish TPNCD as a distinct, necrotic cell death pathway underlying acute liver injury and highlight new therapeutic entry points for hepatoprotection.

title: CRISPR mutagenesis of the MYC locus reveals a druggable ultraconserved RNA element
